entry.title: InfluxDB 3: A Source Tour of the Rust, Arrow, and Parquet Time-Series Engine

link.title: InfluxDB 3: A Source Tour of the Rust, Arrow, and Parquet Time-Series Engine

entry.content:
Anyone who has trained a model or operated a GPU cluster knows the feeling: the metrics are everywhere and the answers are nowhere. GPU utilization counters, temperature probes, token latencies, loss curves from experiment trackers, queue depths from an inference server — all of it arrives as small, append-heavy, time-ordered records, all of it wants to be written right now, and most questions you ask later are about “the most recent value” or “the last hour.” That workload profile is exactly what a time-series database (TSDB) is built for, which is why TSDBs sit underneath ML platforms: they absorb telemetry at line rate and answer dashboards, alerts, and drift checks without a full-scan tax. If you have read our tours of VictoriaMetrics, TimescaleDB, or ClickHouse, you know how differently each system answers that question.

InfluxDB 3 Core is InfluxData’s answer, rebuilt from the ground up. The project describes itself as “powered by Apache Arrow, DataFusion, and Parquet”: writes arrive as InfluxDB line protocol, rows are held as Arrow RecordBatches in memory, queries run through the DataFusion engine, and the durable format is Parquet files on object storage — S3, Azure, GCP buckets, or just the local disk with no dependencies. The project has been generally available since April 2025, and its feature list reads like a wishlist for observability on a budget: a diskless architecture with object storage support, sub-10 ms last-value queries from an in-memory cache, an embedded Python VM for plugins and triggers, and compatibility with the 1.x/2.x write APIs and the InfluxQL query language.

One clarification before we dive in: the default branch of influxdata/influxdb on GitHub is main, and that branch hosts the InfluxDB 3 Core codebase — a Rust workspace of about thirty crates. The older, pre-Rewrite generations of InfluxDB live on separate branches of the same repository: the 2.x code (Go and Flux, with its TSM storage engine) is on main-2.x, and the venerable 1.x code is on master-1.x. Nothing in this tour touches those branches; every file and line number below comes from the Rust code on main, verified directly against the working tree; the two diagrams below were generated from that same tree.

Overview of InfluxDB 3 Core on the main branch: the influxdb3 binary wires an HTTP API, a write buffer, Parquet persistence, and a DataFusion-backed query executor into one server.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • fn main, L4 is the entry point of the influxdb3 server binary, which fans out into clap-based subcommands.
  • command, L952 is the serve command: it resolves configuration, constructs the object store, and assembles the runtime.
  • HttpApi, L1040 holds the two halves of the system — a write_buffer and a query_executor — behind one HTTP interface.
  • API_V3_WRITE, L5 names the /api/v3/write_lp route; sibling constants define /api/v3/query_sql, /api/v2/write, and the legacy /write endpoints.
  • WriteBufferImpl, L170 is the ingest heart: it validates line protocol rows, appends them to the WAL, and hands them to the queryable buffer.
  • QueryableBuffer, L44 keeps recent data as in-memory Arrow chunks and doubles as the WAL’s file notifier.
  • Persister, L128 is, in the code’s own words, “the primary interface with object storage where InfluxDB stores all Parquet.”
  • QueryExecutorImpl, L61 wraps the DataFusion/IOx execution layer so SQL and InfluxQL plans can read both buffered chunks and persisted Parquet.

The detailed view adds the CLI flags, route dispatch, WAL mechanics, per-table buffers, and the Parquet persistence calls that the overview collapses into single boxes.

The Write Path: Line Protocol to WalOp

Everything starts with an HTTP POST. The route_request, L2671 dispatch table matches (Method::POST, API_V3_WRITE) to the write handler, and write_lp, L1107 pulls parameters — db, precision, accept_partial, no_sync — straight from the URL query string. write_lp_inner, L1113 validates the database name, decodes the UTF-8 body, and calls into the buffer with the server’s clock as the default timestamp.

Inside the buffer, write_lp, L464 parses and validates the line protocol, and write_lp_inner, L505 converts valid lines into buffered data. The interesting commitment comes next: valid rows become a WalOp::Write, L541 and are pushed through write_ops_unconfirmed, L544. The comment in the code explains the contract — the WAL buffers ops in memory and, once per flush interval (about a second by default), persists them as a single WAL file in the configured object store. When that happens, the QueryableBuffer, L44 is notified: it was registered as the WAL’s file_notifier at construction time (L429), and its buffer_write_ops, L575 applies the batch into per-table buffers. The TableBuffer, L46 chunks by time (buffer_chunk, L113) and can turn any chunk into partitioned Arrow RecordBatches on demand — so data is queryable within milliseconds, long before it is durable as Parquet. Replay on restart follows the same edges in reverse: the WAL instance is created only after the persisted snapshot list is loaded, then feeds the buffer back into a queryable state.

From Line Protocol to Parquet: The Storage Side

The WAL is the short-term journal; Parquet is the long-term memory. Snapshots are the hinge between them: persist_snapshot, L370 writes the snapshot’s file list to object storage, which is what allows old WAL files to be dropped. The actual conversion happens in serialize_to_parquet, L202, which runs an Arrow ArrowWriter over the RecordBatches, and persist_parquet_file, L986, which writes those bytes to the object store and returns metadata used to prime the parquet cache. The PersistedFiles, L28 index tracks what has already landed, grouped by month, so the query planner can prune files it does not need.

Two design choices stand out. First, file paths are prefixed by the node identifier — the --node-id flag (L794) exists precisely so multiple servers sharing one bucket do not collide. Second, this OSS workspace persists “Gen1” Parquet files and stops there: there is no compactor crate in the tree you clone from main. Background compaction (merging Gen1 files into larger, query-optimized files) is part of the commercial InfluxDB 3 Enterprise story, and the open-source tree simply does not include it. The Persister, L128 also owns the read side of storage with load_parquet_file, L361 — worth remembering when you wonder who fetches cold data back.

The Query Side: DataFusion Over Everything

On reads, InfluxDB 3 Core is essentially an Arrow-native SQL engine with two data sources stitched together. QueryExecutorImpl, L61 holds the IOx/DataFusion Executor and a per-database Database, L532 registry that exposes each table’s buffered chunks and Parquet files to the planner. Execution bottoms out in execute_stream, L339, where the session context streams RecordBatches out of the physical plan. The HTTP handler query_sql, L1198 accepts GET with db and q URL parameters or POST with a JSON body, and renders results as pretty tables, CSV, JSON, or Parquet. A gRPC side exists too: the FlightSQL service in grpc.rs, L12 lets Arrow-native clients run the same plans over the Flight protocol, and an InfluxQL compatibility layer translates the old 1.x query language. The README’s claim of last-value queries under 10 ms comes from this layer’s distinct-value and last-value caches — QueryableBuffer, L44 collaborates with the distinct and last cache managers that the WriteBuffer trait composes in lib.rs, L66.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps installation honest: Docker images, Debian and RPM packages, and tarballs are on the InfluxData downloads page, and both Core and Enterprise have getting-started guides on docs.influxdata.com. Building from source is documented in CONTRIBUTING.md for contributors. Once installed, the server binary is influxdb3, and the serve command wires everything you saw above. The essential flags, all verified in the CLI definitions: --node-id names the node and prefixes every object store path; --object-store file selects the local filesystem as storage (per the crate’s own docs you must also set --data-dir, which defaults to a .influxdb3 directory); and --http-bind controls the listener, defaulting to 0.0.0.0:8181 per DEFAULT_HTTP_BIND_ADDR, L101. For a throwaway local experiment you can add --without-auth (L319); otherwise the server provisions an admin token through create_admin_token, L1150 on first start. A GET /health endpoint exists for readiness checks.

With the server listening on port 8181, your first write uses the route we traced: POST line protocol to /api/v3/write_lp with a db query parameter. Feeding it a GPU-telemetry-shaped line is the natural demo:

curl -X POST 'http://localhost:8181/api/v3/write_lp?db=demo' \
  -d 'gpu_temp,host=h0,gpu=a100_1 value=71.5'

The response is HTTP 204 when every line was valid — the handler returns the empty body path only when invalid_lines is empty, and otherwise reports the partial write failure. Then query it back with SQL over /api/v3/query_sql, where db selects the database and q carries the SQL text (both names are serde renames on the request struct, so they apply to GET and POST alike):

curl 'http://localhost:8181/api/v3/query_sql?db=demo&q=SELECT+*+FROM+gpu_temp'

What makes this loop satisfying for ML telemetry specifically: the measurement you just created behaves like a table immediately, and the same SQL runs against the hot buffer and the cold Parquet without you choosing. Point your training script’s metrics at /api/v3/write_lp, point Grafana or a notebook at /api/v3/query_sql, and you have a complete “your first model” story: a durable, queryable record of how every experiment behaved.

How the Catalog Holds It Together

One more crate deserves a paragraph: the catalog. Every write and every query touches metadata — which databases exist, which tables belong to them, column types, retention policies. The write buffer exposes it via catalog, L793, returning an Arc<Catalog> from the influxdb3_catalog crate, and the HTTP layer leans on it for token management too. This is a deliberate architectural split in the 3.x design: the catalog is serialized metadata that survives independently of the data files, and the write path consults it to validate incoming lines before any WAL op exists. The trait layering in the write crate — WriteBuffer composing Bufferer, ChunkContainer, DistinctCacheManager, and LastCacheManager from lib.rs, L66 — keeps that metadata-adjacent logic swappable and testable. For the server assembly itself, Server, L151 is built from a CreateServerArgs bundle and serve, L366 drives the accept loop — the final edge in our detail diagram.

Honest Limits

No source tour is complete without the fine print, and InfluxDB 3 Core has a clear one: what you clone from main is the open-source single-node core, and the clustering, replication, and compaction machinery that large deployments want live in the separate, closed-source Enterprise product — the README is explicit that the commercial code is kept separate, and links distinct getting-started guides for Core and Enterprise. Concretely, the OSS tree persists Gen1 Parquet files and relies on the WAL and caches for speed; you will not find a compactor crate here. Second, version archaeology in this repository is unusual: main is InfluxDB 3 Core in Rust, main-2.x is the 2.x generation (the Go/Flux era), and master-1.x is the original 1.x engine — same repository, three different databases. If you are migrating an old 1.x/2.x deployment, the compatibility write APIs and InfluxQL ease that jump, but the storage engines share nothing. Finally, the numbers in this post are code-verified structure, not benchmarks: the README’s sub-10 ms last-value claim is the vendor’s, and your cardinality, disk, and hardware will decide your truth. For adjacent reading, our DuckDB tour pairs well here if you want a second Arrow-native engine to compare against.

entry.title: Jaeger: Tracing Every Hop of Your Distributed AI Stack

link.title: Jaeger: Tracing Every Hop of Your Distributed AI Stack

entry.content:
Modern AI systems are distributed systems in disguise. A single “ask the model a question” request in a production RAG application usually touches an API gateway, an embedding service, a vector database, a retriever, maybe a reranker, and finally an LLM provider — and if you add agents into the mix, each tool call fans out into further network hops. When a user complains that answers are slow or wrong, a stack trace in one service tells you almost nothing. What you need is a trace: a tree of timed spans showing exactly where the 8 seconds went — 200 ms in retrieval, 6.5 s waiting on the model, 1.2 s re-serializing context you did not need.

That is the problem Jaeger was built to solve. Originally created at Uber and later donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, Jaeger is the most widely deployed open-source distributed tracing platform in the Go ecosystem, and the natural landing zone for traces from an instrumented FastAPI service or any OTel SDK. In 2024 the project shipped Jaeger v2, a fundamental architectural shift: the backend was rebuilt as an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution, so ingestion, sampling, and storage are all expressed as standard OTel components instead of bespoke services. If your app already exports OTLP, retargeting it at Jaeger is usually a one-line environment variable change.

In this post we tour the actual source code of jaegertracing/jaeger on the main branch, following a span from ingest endpoint to rendered UI. Both diagrams below were generated directly from the repository, so every node links to the real source file on GitHub.

Jaeger v2 at a glance: one binary, standard OTel receivers on the left, pluggable storage in the middle, and the query/UI stack on the right, with a standalone remote-storage gRPC server for hybrid deployments.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main(), L12 — the single jaeger binary is an OTel Collector distribution; its entry point just wires factories and executes the command.
  • Components(), L28 — returns the full component set the standard binary ships with, which custom distributions can extend.
  • all-in-one.yaml, L70 — the embedded default configuration accepts OTLP over gRPC on port 4317 and HTTP on 4318, plus legacy Jaeger thrift and Zipkin endpoints.
  • processTraces, L68 — before storage, the adaptive sampling processor recalculates per-operation sampling probabilities from live traffic.
  • TraceWriter, L25 — the write step behind jaeger_storage_exporter: sanitize each OTLP batch, then hand it to the configured backend.
  • GetTraceStoreFactory, L65 — the jaeger_storage extension resolves a named backend into a tracestore.Factory.
  • NewStore, L43 — with no config flags, the binary runs all-in-one against an in-memory store capped at 100,000 traces.
  • NewServer, L57 — the jaeger_query extension binds the HTTP and gRPC query servers on one port.
  • NewQueryService, L129 — the query service wraps any backend reader with search rules, pagination, and archive support.

The detailed map: bootstrap chain, the write path from receivers through the storage exporter, the pluggable backends, the remote-storage gRPC server, and the query/AI surface.

From Install to Your First Trace

The README’s quick start is genuinely two commands long. Run the all-in-one image, which bundles the UI, the collector-side components, the query server, and in-memory storage:

docker run --rm --name jaeger \
  -p 16686:16686 \
  -p 4317:4317 \
  -p 4318:4318 \
  jaegertracing/jaeger:latest

Open http://localhost:16686 for the UI, then point any OpenTelemetry SDK at OTLP gRPC port 4317 or OTLP/HTTP port 4318. If your app already exports OTLP to another backend, you can usually retarget it with one environment variable. Within seconds your service appears in the UI’s service dropdown, and clicking a trace shows the familiar waterfall of spans with per-span timings, tags, logs, and process metadata.

The UI is not the only consumer. The query extension registers a classic JSON API under the default prefix api — see RegisterRoutes, L105 for the route table, including GET /api/traces/{id}, /api/dependencies, and the SPM metrics endpoints. The v2 codebase also serves API v3, an OTLP-native contract: RegisterRoutes, L51 mounts /api/v3/traces and friends on OTLP protobuf types directly, so an LLM analysis tool can consume raw ptrace.Traces without translating Jaeger’s legacy model.

One curl against the JSON API is enough to confirm the flow works headlessly: fetch a trace ID from your app’s tracer output, then curl http://localhost:16686/api/traces/<traceID> and inspect the JSON. Note that in-memory storage means everything evaporates on container restart — fine for development, and the reason production runs swap in a real backend, which we do next.

Inside the v2 Binary: an OTel Collector Distribution

The most interesting thing about Jaeger v2 is what it no longer contains. There is no custom collector daemon: cmd/jaeger builds an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution. main(), L12 calls Components(), L28, which delegates to the registry in cmd/jaeger/internal/components.go — that file registers the OTLP, Jaeger, Zipkin, and Kafka receivers, a set of exporters, and five Jaeger-specific extensions: jaeger_query, jaeger_storage, remote_sampling, expvar, and remotestorage.

Bootstrap behavior lives in NewCommand, L32. The command intercepts the collector’s RunE: if no --config flag was passed, checkConfigAndRun injects the embedded all-in-one.yaml, which is why docker run jaegertracing/jaeger:latest works with zero configuration. Pass your own config and you compose the same components differently — receivers on one port, a tail-sampling processor in the middle, storage elsewhere.

This design is a gift for LLM infrastructure teams. It means one config file describes your whole tracing topology, and the same binary can play collector, query server, or remote-storage role depending on which extensions you enable. Compare that with wiring three separate services, and the appeal for compact Kubernetes deployments becomes obvious.

The Write Path: From Receiver to Storage

Follow a batch of spans inward. After a receiver accepts them, the jaeger_storage_exporter is the last stop. Its TraceWriter, L25 resolves the configured storage at startup in Start, L43 by calling GetTraceStoreFactory, L65, which locates the jaeger_storage extension in the collector host. At runtime, WriteTraces, L112 runs each batch through a sanitizer and forwards it verbatim to the backend.

Everything downstream of that call implements one contract: tracestore.Writer, L14, an OTLP-compatible, idempotent WriteTraces(ctx, td). The interface is documented with unusual care — implementations must write synchronously or explicitly document an asynchronous mode, because the Kafka ingester needs real errors for backpressure and retry. That kind of contract-first thinking is why Jaeger backends stay swappable.

The extension resolves factories lazily in TraceStorageFactory, L184, caching each one, and the shared switch in CreateTraceStorageFactory, L32 maps config to concrete backends. On the v2 storage tree you get: the in-memory store (NewStore, L43, writing via a per-tenant clone at L72), Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (NewFactory, L44, with reader and writer factories at L60 and L66), Cassandra, ClickHouse, Badger, and a gRPC remote backend. Legacy v1 plugins are bridged through adapters like NewTraceWriter, L32, so the long tail of third-party storage plugins keeps working while the ecosystem migrates.

For high-volume deployments the repo ships config variants like config-kafka-collector.yaml and config-kafka-ingester.yaml: collectors export spans into Kafka, and an ingester consumes them into storage. This decouples ingest latency spikes — a burst of agent tool-call traces, say — from your database’s write capacity.

The Read Path: Query APIs, the UI, and MCP Tools for AI Agents

On the serving side, NewServer, L57 builds both an HTTP server and a gRPC server — same port, shared interceptors for bearer tokens and tenancy. registerGRPCHandlers, L98 registers the v2 jaeger.api_v2.QueryService and the v3 service on one gRPC endpoint, and initRouter mounts the API v3 gateway, the classic JSON API, the static UI assets, and a growing set of AI routes.

The domain logic lives in the query service: NewQueryService, L129 wraps any backend reader; GetTraces, L160 fetches by ID; FindTraces, L228 runs searches, normalizing the query in prepareSearchQuery, L280 — which refuses searches without a service name unless the backend advertises support, and enforces time-range bounds. Dependencies for the service graph come from GetDependencies, L569. On the HTTP side, getTrace, L335 is the handler your curl hit earlier.

The genuinely new capability is aimed at agents, not humans. Under /api/ai/, Register, L63 mounts an AI gateway whose MCP endpoint is served by NewHandler, L116 — an MCP server exposing tools like search_traces, get_trace_topology, get_critical_path, and error-root-cause skills over the query service. In other words, your coding agent can now query production traces through the Model Context Protocol the same way it reads files. For anyone building LLM observability alongside evaluation tooling like Opik or workflow analysis with Phoenix, a tracing backend that speaks MCP natively is a meaningful shortcut: the agent gets ground truth about latencies and failures instead of guessed-at logs.

Scaling Out: Remote Storage, Sampling, and Honest Topology Options

Two mechanisms make Jaeger scale beyond one container. First, adaptive sampling: the processor at processTraces, L68 watches operation throughput and adjusts per-route sampling probabilities, served back to SDKs through the remote_sampling extension on ports 5778 (HTTP) and 5779 (gRPC) per the embedded config. High-traffic services send fewer spans; rare operations keep full fidelity.

Second, the remote-storage gRPC server decouples old and new worlds. The v2 binary can embed it via the remotestorage extension — see Start, L37 — and there is also a standalone cmd/remote-storage binary whose NewServer, L40 wraps any backend into gRPC handlers via grpcstorage.NewHandler, L65, registered on the server at L116. The wire contract matches the client factory at NewFactory, L47, whose handler exposes GetTraces, Export, and GetDependencies in handler.go, L48. Practical takeaway: you can keep v1-era agents and collectors in place, front them with a v2 remote-storage pod, and migrate storage underneath without touching application code.

Honest Limits

  • In-memory storage is development-only. The default store caps at 100,000 traces and vanishes on restart. Production requires running Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Cassandra, or ClickHouse — each a real operational commitment. If you only need metrics rather than traces, a time-series stack is far cheaper to operate.
  • Storage costs grow with cardinality. Tracing every LLM call with full prompts and completions as span attributes will bloat Elasticsearch or ClickHouse fast. Sample deliberately, and keep payload blobs in object storage with trace IDs as pointers.
  • v1 to v2 migration is real work. The repo carries both generations — legacy cmd components were removed in v2, but many deployments still run v1 binaries alongside v2 remote storage. Version skew, config translation, and dual-running are documented but non-trivial.
  • Spans are not evaluations. Jaeger tells you what happened and how long it took; it will not tell you whether the model’s answer was good. Pair it with an evaluation layer, and use the new MCP tools as the bridge rather than a replacement.
  • Single-binary mode has no HA story. All-in-one is a single process; meaningful deployments need the collector/query separation (or at least external storage) plus health checks — the config exposes healthcheckv2 on 13133 for exactly that.

For AI engineering teams, the pitch condenses to this: your stack already emits OTLP; Jaeger v2 ingests it with commodity collector config, stores it in whichever database your platform team tolerates, and now — through its MCP server — lets your agents interrogate production latency themselves. That last part is the newest idea in the codebase — and the most likely to change how you debug multi-hop LLM systems.

entry.title: Grafana Loki: Log Aggregation That Indexes Labels, Not Lines

link.title: Grafana Loki: Log Aggregation That Indexes Labels, Not Lines

entry.content:
If you have ever trained a model overnight and woken up to a cryptic CUDA OOM at 3 a.m., you already know the real product of an ML system is not just the checkpoint — it is the log trail. Training jobs emit loss curves, data-loader warnings, NCCL timeout errors and GPU driver messages scattered across dozens of pods. Inference servers add request traces, latency warnings and quantization diagnostics on top. When something breaks, grep-ing SSH sessions across a dozen machines is not debugging, it is archaeology. Centralized log aggregation is the unglamorous infrastructure that turns that archaeology into a search box.

The catch is cost. Traditional log platforms build a full-text inverted index over every word you ship, which means storing roughly as much index as logs — often more. Grafana Loki takes the opposite road. Its README describes it in one line: “Loki: like Prometheus, but for logs.” Like Prometheus for metrics, Loki indexes only labels — the small key/value pairs such as job, app or pod that identify a stream — and stores the log lines themselves compressed and unindexed. Searching inside lines happens at query time, by scanning. That trade makes the write path fast, the storage bill small, and the operational burden light, at the price of slower full-text scans. Queries reuse the exact label vocabulary you already use for metrics, and if you run Grafana you can flip between metrics and logs without changing mental models.

This post is a source tour of the Loki repository (branch main, module github.com/grafana/loki/v3), focused on the Go code that makes that idea real: the distributor that receives your logs, the ingester that buffers and flushes them, the LogQL engine that answers queries, and the storage layer that indexes labels and nothing else. I mapped both the write path and the read path into two diagrams; every symbol cited below was located in the actual source at a verified line number.

Overview: one binary, four roles. The module manager wires the push handler, ingester, querier, LogQL engine and ruler over a shared TSDB index and object storage.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L138 — the cmd/loki binary parses its config wrapper and calls loki.New, then t.Run at L149 starts every service for the selected -target.
  • Loki struct, L446 — the root datastructure holding the server, ring, overrides and every component; setupModuleManager at L798 builds the dependency graph between modules.
  • initDistributor, L341 — wires the push HTTP handler at L393 and routes POST /loki/api/v1/push at L403.
  • Distributor.Push, L508 — the write entry point: validates each stream, shards streams by label hash and replicates them to ingesters over gRPC.
  • instance.Push, L231 — the per-tenant ingester instance appends entries into compressed in-memory chunks and logs a record to the WAL at L265.
  • query.Exec, L273 — the LogQL engine executes instant and range queries, deferring to an evaluator built by NewDefaultEvaluator at L310.
  • SelectLogs, L217 — the querier merges still-buffered logs from ingesters with long-term store reads; SelectSamples at L290 serves the metric side of LogQL.
  • NewStore, L132 — the LokiStore (type at L99) fans each query out over schema periods, using a per-period index and chunk client.

Detail view: from HTTP push and the distributor's validation flow, through ingester streams, chunk cuts and the WAL, into the LogQL engine, querier fan-out, TSDB index and object storage.

From Install to Your First Model

Loki ships as a single Go binary with no external dependencies, which is exactly what you want when the machines you care about are GPU nodes that should not be running a zookeeper of their own. The README’s build-from-source path is three commands: clone the repository, build with go build ./cmd/loki, and run ./loki -config.file=./cmd/loki/loki-local-config.yaml (both commands are shown verbatim in the repository README, lines 108-111). The checked-in local config listens on http_listen_port: 3100 (line 4 of cmd/loki/loki-local-config.yaml), which is the one port you need to remember; gRPC sits next to it on 9096.

Readiness is a plain HTTP check: the root Loki struct registers a GET /ready handler at loki.go L638 that flips to 200 once all modules report healthy. In a Kubernetes launcher this is your startup probe. Getting logs in is a single HTTP call — the push route is the constant PathLokiPush = "/loki/api/v1/push" defined at api_paths.go L34 — and the same endpoint accepts OpenTelemetry payloads through a dedicated OTLP handler at http.go L36, so an OpenTelemetry Collector sidecar can forward trace-adjacent log records without any Loki-specific agent. The repository README also documents LogCLI, a small command-line client for running queries like a stream selector against your instance.

Your first query is then a label selector. In LogQL, curly braces pick streams the way they do in PromQL: something like a selector on job or pod returns every line of those streams in the time range, and you can layer filters and metric expressions on top — wrap the selector in rate(...) or count matches per minute — without ever leaving the same query language your dashboards use. For a training fleet this pays off immediately: one query template per job name surfaces driver errors from every node, and the same labels that showed you GPU utilization in Prometheus now show you the logs around each spike.

Inside the Write Path: Distributor to Ingester

A push request lands at the distributor, and the first thing that happens is not storage — it is judgment. Distributor.Push at L508 resolves the tenant from the context and hands the request to pushWithResolver at L520, which walks every stream, enforces per-tenant limits such as ingestion rate and label length, optionally shards streams that exceed their rate budget, and computes each stream’s hash key from its labels. The hash is what the consistent ring uses to pick which ingester replicas own the stream. Rejected streams never leave the distributor, and the response reports what was dropped.

The receiving ingester is deliberately simple: Ingester.Push at ingester.go L1018 checks whether the WAL disk is throttled, then dispatches to a per-tenant instance. Inside the instance at instance.go L231, streams are looked up or created — createStream at L283 parses the label set and applies stream-count limits — and entries are appended by stream.Push at stream.go L168. Lines accumulate in a compressed in-memory chunk; when the chunk fills, cutChunk at L492 seals it for the flusher. Before any of that is acked, the instance writes a record to the WAL (wal.Log call at instance.go L265), so a crash between memory and object storage costs you nothing. The WAL interface itself lives at wal.go L63.

Two design choices matter here. First, chunks are grouped by label set: all lines with identical labels share a stream, which is why high-cardinality labels blow up both memory and index — a theme the limits section returns to. Second, the write path is O(labels), not O(lines): line text is only compressed, never parsed for indexing, so the cost per gigabyte stays flat no matter how chatty your training logs are.

Inside the Read Path: LogQL Down to Chunks

Queries enter through the same module wiring but take the opposite route. The querier module (initQuerier at modules.go L520) builds a query API at L642 and instantiates the LogQL engine via logql.NewEngine at L2298. The engine type at engine.go L208 parses your query into an AST (ParseExpr at syntax/parser.go L62), then query.Exec at L273 instruments the run and delegates to the evaluator, which pulls data through the Querier interface.

The SingleTenantQuerier (type at querier.go L165) is the fan-out point, and its constructor signature at L186 is a quiet announcement of the storage transition: it takes both a classic chunk store and a new data-object store. For log queries, SelectLogs at L217 merges two sources — the IngesterQuerier (type at ingester_querier.go L50), which asks live ingesters for unflushed streams, and the long-term store. Metric queries call SelectSamples at L290 with the same dual sources. The merge means Loki answers over the last few minutes and the last few months with one query and no special-casing in your dashboard.

Storage: Index the Labels, Compress the Lines

The store is where the “index only labels” promise is kept. LokiStore at store.go L99 is schema-aware: Loki’s config lets different time periods use different index and chunk backends, and NewStore at L132 assembles a client per period. SelectLogs at L531 walks the period configs that overlap the query range, and each one consults the index — the TSDB single-store index whose builder lives under pkg/storage/stores/shipper/indexshipper/tsdb/builder.go — to turn label matchers into a list of chunk references. Only then are the referenced objects fetched, through the chunk client built by NewChunkClient at factory.go L354 on top of the object client from NewObjectClient at L415 (S3, GCS, Azure, or plain filesystem — a MinIO bucket works fine for a homelab). The index is small because it maps labels and stream time ranges, not words; the chunks are big but cheap because they are just compressed bytes.

The tree also shows where the project is heading. A columnar object format lives at pkg/dataobj/dataobj.go (the Object type at L89), with builder, compaction and metastore modules registered in the module table — a storage engine that keeps data in open columnar objects instead of the classic chunk-plus-index split. Bloom filters for line-level pruning ship under pkg/storage/bloom/v1 with a dedicated shipper. The ruler — built by NewRuler at ruler.go L14 and wired at modules.go L1458 — reuses the exact same LogQL engine (see createRulerQueryEngine touching the engine at L1548), so the query you debug interactively is the query your alert evaluates on a schedule.

Honest Limits

Loki’s economy has a price, and it is worth naming before you commit a fleet to it. Label-only indexing means anything inside the line is found by scanning: a query that filters on a rare string across a week of logs will touch far more data than the same search in ClickHouse, which indexes aggressively and answers ad-hoc full-text in milliseconds — but pays for that with a heavier cluster and a real database to operate. If your workflow is “grep anything, anytime, forever,” Loki will feel slow at large ranges. If it is “show me logs for this pod around the CPU spike,” it feels instant.

The second limit is cardinality, self-inflicted by design. Every unique label combination is a stream with its own index entries and its own in-memory buffer, so slapping a UUID or a request ID into labels multiplies streams until the ingester rejects writes. The rule of thumb the project repeats: keep identifiers in the log line, keep stable attributes in labels. Third, WAL-replay restarts are real: an ingester that crashes replays its WAL before serving, and while replication covers you, a monolithic single-binary deployment trades that safety for simplicity. Fourth, the repository is in visible motion — the distributor/ingester/querier packages have just moved out of pkg/loki to the repository root (pkg/distributor, pkg/ingester, pkg/querier), and the data-object storage engine is under active construction, so file paths in this tour will drift with the tree. None of that changes the core bet: for ML teams that already run Prometheus and Grafana, Loki turns the log trail of a failed training run into a label query — and keeps the storage bill small enough that you can afford to keep every epoch’s logs.

entry.title: Inside Memcached: The C Event Machine That Still Wins the Latency Game

link.title: Inside Memcached: The C Event Machine That Still Wins the Latency Game

entry.content:
If you build anything around models, you spend your life answering the same question over and over: the same prompt prefix, the same tokenizer call, the same feature vector, the same session lookup. Doing that work twice is pure waste, and at inference scale waste is measured in GPUs. That is why the humble in-memory cache is quietly one of the most load-bearing components of modern ML infrastructure: an embedding cache turns repeated encoding requests into sub-millisecond hash lookups, a tokenization cache keeps your preprocessor from re-splitting the same corpus a thousand times, and a session store keeps state off stateless inference servers. Before Redis, before Valkey, there was Memcached — and its C source is still one of the best teaching artifacts in open source.

Memcached describes itself as a “high performance multithreaded event-based key/value cache store intended to be used in a distributed system”, and the entire project fits in a handful of C files at the root of the repository. There is no scripting engine in the core, no persistence by default, no clusters-from-the-box. The philosophy is radical simplicity: hash a key, find an item, hand it back, and evict old data when memory runs out. Everything else — consistency, partitioning, serialization — is deliberately left to the client. That refusal to grow is exactly why it remains a default choice for LRU-style caching fleets two decades in.

This post walks the actual source tree on master with two generated architecture diagrams: an overview of the request flow, and a deeper map covering the protocols, memory management, flash offload, LRU crawler and the newer proxy layer. Every symbol below is linked to its real line on GitHub, so you can read along in the code as we go.

The overview: a client connection is accepted, handed to a worker thread, parsed by the text or meta protocol layer, and answered from the slab-allocated hash table — with a flash fallback for oversized items.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L4714 parses flags like -p, -m and -t, initializes the slab allocator and threads, then settles into the libevent loop that never returns.
  • conn_new, L610 wraps each accepted socket in a conn struct and attaches it to an event base; this is also where proxy-mode connections get their own read handler installed.
  • drive_machine, L2965 is the beating heart: a while (!stop) loop that walks a connection through listening, waiting, reading, parsing and writing states.
  • dispatch_conn_new, L772 spreads new connections across worker threads via their notify pipes, so no single thread owns the listening socket queue.
  • process_command_ascii, L1529 is the dispatcher for both the classic text protocol and the modern meta commands (mg, ms, md, ma, me).
  • do_item_alloc, L249 carves a new item out of the slab allocator sized to the key-plus-value, while do_slabs_alloc, L411 hands out the actual chunk.
  • assoc_find, L70 walks the chained hash bucket for the key — the single most executed data structure operation in the daemon.

The detail map: protocols and parsers on one side, slab and LRU machinery in the middle, and the extstore flash path, LRU crawler and Lua proxy at the edges.

The Event Loop Is a State Machine

Most servers you read will have a handler-per-request structure. Memcached does something older and, in my opinion, more elegant: every connection is a tiny state machine, and drive_machine, L2965 is the single function that advances all of them. The switch (c->state) covers conn_listening (accept with accept4), conn_waiting, conn_read (via try_read_network, L2431), conn_parse_cmd, conn_nread (copying the value bytes into the item with complete_nread, L1422), conn_mwrite and conn_closing.

Two details in that loop reward attention. First, conn_new_cmd decrements a per-event request budget (nreqs, seeded from settings.reqs_per_event) so a single chatty connection cannot starve the rest of the worker — the loop yields and lets libevent re-arm instead. Second, the same state machine drives listener sockets and client sockets alike; a listening conn simply sits in conn_listening and accepts, then dispatch_conn_new ships the client fd to a worker. The threading model is one lock-free event loop per worker thread, each owning a slice of connections, with a short mutexed section whenever the shared hash table is touched. It is the original “threads plus epoll” recipe, and reading it makes most modern async frameworks look overdressed.

One Daemon, Three Dialects

The protocol surface is where the code has grown the most, and the dispatcher process_command_ascii, L1529 shows all of it in one switch. Parsing itself was recently unified in process_request, L163, a shared tokenizer that extracts the key, flags, TTL and value length for both classic and meta commands.

The classic text protocol is still what most people learn first: get, set, gets route through process_get_command, L429 and process_update_command, L764, the latter calling into the shared process_update_cmd_start in the parser which allocates the item before the value bytes are read. The meta protocol (mg, ms, md, ma, me, mn) is the modern surface — compact, flag-driven, and finally able to express things like “return TTL with the value” or “vivify the key if missing” without new verbs. The mg path in process_mget_cmd, L984 is worth reading in full: flag letters (v, f, t, c, k, N, J) each map to behavior, including on-the-fly item creation for the vivify case.

The binary protocol lives in proto_bin.c, where try_read_command_binary, L49 validates the fixed 24-byte header and dispatch_bin_command, L897 switches over opcodes, including the SASL authentication commands. And since this is a cache used in front of fleets, there is a fourth dialect that is not even a client dialect: when the server is built with --enable-proxy (documented in the README), proxy-mode connections get try_read_command_proxy, L605 installed as their read handler, and requests flow into the Lua-based router instead of the local hash table.

Slabs, LRU and the Hash Table

Memory management is the part of Memcached that has barely changed since the beginning, because it is hard to beat. The allocator slabs.c pre-sorts memory into slab classes, each holding pages carved into fixed-size chunks; the growth factor and minimum chunk size are the -f and -n flags you see in usage, L4008. When a value needs storing, do_item_alloc, L249 asks do_slabs_alloc, L411 for a chunk from the right class, and when items die, do_slabs_free, L501 returns the chunk to its freelist. No coalescing, no compaction — fragmentation is contained by design because chunks within a class are uniform.

On top of the allocator sits a classic pair: a chained hash table and per-LRU-class eviction. The hash function is pluggable at startup via hash_init, L15 — jenkins, murmur3 or the modern xxh3 default — and inserts go through assoc_insert, L153 while lookups walk buckets in assoc_find, L70. The item itself is linked into an LRU by do_item_link, L485, and when memory is tight or items expire, lru_pull_tail, L1072 sweeps the tail of a given LRU: evicting, unlinking through assoc_delete, L172, and recycling the chunk. Refcounts, not locks, keep an item alive while a reader finishes with it — a pattern worth stealing for your own code.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s build instructions are refreshingly short, and they still work. For a from-source build you need autotools and libevent (on Debian: sudo apt-get install autotools-dev automake libevent-dev), then:

cd memcached
./autogen.sh
./configure
make
make test

The binary lands in the same folder. Start it with a memory cap and a thread count tuned to your box — -m sets item memory in megabytes, -t the worker threads, -p the TCP port (defaults to 11211), all documented in the usage text:

./memcached -m 2048 -t 4 -p 11211 -u nobody

Then the README’s own smoke test: telnet 127.0.0.1 11211 and type stats. Because the text protocol is exactly that — text — your first cache round-trip needs nothing more than a shell. Once connected, set greeting 0 0 5 followed by hello stores a value, and get greeting brings it back; you can see every one of these verbs handled in proto_text.c. From Python, a two-line client (telnetlib for a demo, or pymemcache in production) is enough to front your tokenizer or embedding service with a shared fleet: point several app servers at one host string, and keys collide into a single namespace. For the AI workloads above the sweet spot is exactly what the code shows: hot, small, immutable values with a TTL. If you need persistence, streams or rich data types, that is a different tool — see the tour of Redis or its libre fork Valkey — and if you are wiring the cache into request handlers, the FastAPI source tour shows the app side of that integration.

Flash, Crawler, Proxy: The Modern Edges

Three newer subsystems extend the classic core without contaminating it. The first is extstore, enabled with --enable-extstore and isolated in extstore.c: a background writer thread in storage_write, L499 pulls cold items off the COLD_LRU tail, allocates a tiny header item to stay in RAM, and streams the body to flash pages through extstore_write, L652. A read of such an item goes through storage_get_item, L252, which submits an async I/O back into the event loop — RAM prices be damned, this is how you keep a 100 GB embedding cache without 100 GB of DRAM.

The second is the LRU crawler in crawler.c: instead of letting expiration happen lazily on access, lru_crawler metadump or lru_crawler crawl all (parsed by process_lru_crawler_command, L1287 and started in lru_crawler_crawl, L933) walks LRU tails in the background, expiring dead items and even streaming key metadata for debugging.

The third is the proxy layer under proto_proxy.c and its siblings: once enabled, proxy_process_command, L966 builds a request object and runs it through proxy_run_rcontext, L818, a Lua execution context where you write routing functions — pool selection, key prefixing, retries, shadow reads. It turns a fleet of memcached boxes into one logical cache with client-side unawareness, which for large embedding stores is the difference between one hot node and a ring.

Honest Limits

Memcached is honest about what it is not, and so should you be. There is no persistence and no replication: restart the daemon and the cache is empty by definition, which is why warm-up scripts and request coalescing on your app tier matter. There is no server-side cluster coordination — partitioning is done by client hashing, so resizing a fleet historically caused cache misses until consistent hashing (or the proxy with its jump/ring hash modules) entered the picture. Values must fit a slab class; very large blobs waste memory unless extstore is enabled, and the classic 1 MB default value cap still shapes how people model data. Expiration is per-item with a TTL, but there are no key tags or group invalidation in the core, so cache invalidation for a corpus refresh means application-level namespacing. And while the meta protocol is a genuine improvement, huge parts of the internet’s tooling still speak the old text protocol, so you will meet both — usually in the same codebase. Use it for what it is — the fastest boring layer between your model and a recompute — and let the diagram above be your map the next time stats output looks like a wall of numbers.
